qAndA.answer: There are twenty officers in the Durham Police Department.

qAndA.answer: Lavoie argues that national narratives often focus on negative events and generalize about police behavior, while the reality in Durham is that the community and police work together to maintain safety, focusing on helping neighbors and community members.
qAndA.question: What does Lavoie see as a key difference between national narratives about police work and the reality on the ground in Durham?

qAndA.answer: The Durham Police emblem on the cruiser door, featuring a sunrise, which contrasts with the typical national narrative focused on darker aspects of policing.
qAndA.question: What symbol does Lavoie point to on the cruiser door that reinforces his point about the importance of local context?

qAndA.answer: Lavoie wishes people would give officers a chance to prove that they are humans who care about the community, going beyond preconceived notions based on national narratives.
qAndA.question: What does Lavoie say he wishes people would do more often in their interactions with police officers?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I'm John LeVoy, I'm a sergeant with the Durham New Hampshire Police Department
and I've been employed with the Durham Police for the last seven years.
So, a sergeant is a first-line supervisor for the Durham Police.
There are 20 officers in the Durham Police Department of Patrol Supervisors
who each supervise their own shift of patrol officers.
So, we have the normal responsibilities of any patrol officer to go out and patrol
and do motor vehicle enforcement, make arrests, conduct investigations, respond to calls for service.
We also have the added responsibility of managing the officers taking command and control of the
situations that occur on our shifts. Specifically for me, I run the busiest shifts that the Durham Police
have, which is Thursday through Sunday and I work the evening and midnight shifts,
which historically with the University of Population that we have combined that with the town
population and residents that we have makes for our busiest times our most calls for service,
the most priority calls occurred in that time. It's the greatest job in the world and I say that
quite frequently and I've heard a lot of other people say that too and it's easy to get
an officer who's been on for a long time that's salty and says I'm ready for retirement and it's not.
But I discredit that. I think it truly is the best job in the world. I literally come to work
every day having no idea what I am going to do. I can have something set in my mind of a schedule
and things tasked that I want to get done or need to get done and within five minutes of my shift
could be sent to something that I'm tied up on for hours and I get nothing done that I had planned
on doing for the whole day but it's totally exciting. It's high speed, it's very intense and it's
that just not knowing what's next. It keeps you on your toes enough that you don't get bored with it
and if nothing is happening it's a job that you can go out and get involved in things on your own.
I have a freedom of not being tied to a desk. Even as a supervisor I have a lot of administrative
roles where I have to sit at a desk for some of my shift but I'm able to get out and go on the road
and drive around. The Seaco area of New Hampshire is a beautiful vibrant, extremely safe place and
that's not by accident. It's because the community members wanted that way. They help keep that
way and the police respond to things in that manner of helping their neighbors and community
members to keep it safe. It doesn't mean that there are not heinous crimes that happen but
what I think people get caught up on is reading or listening to this national narrative
and it's not at the local level and when they have a contact with us they have a preconceived
notion of how that's about to go or what they should expect and it really should be the opposite
or it should be far better. They should have far better expectations of how they'll be treated
or talk to or how to deal with us and I think a lot of times people forget that we're humans that we
live down the street from you or drive on the same roads that you do go to the same supermarkets.
We have families and even those you know who are younger and maybe haven't started a family yet
still have ties to the community or have grown up in the area and people forget that and I think once
we put this facade on of a uniform and a badge and a gun that they somehow forget that where that
person that they bumped into two hours ago downtown and I'm not a different person because I'm
wearing this. I have a job to do but I'm a human and I like talking to people and having a
conversation about things. We don't fit the national narrative. We aren't those labels and tag
words that people see all the time and just which sometimes people would give us a chance to prove
that or that they would just look and see it. See past what you hear or read on your computer
and go talk to the people that actually work in your community.
